claim: Human fetal development has been associated with brain health at later stages.
source: Human fetal development has been associated with brain health at later stages.
evidence: This is a general statement in the abstract that sets up the research question.

claim: The study included 5794 persons aged 4–82 years at baseline.
source: Here we show remarkably stable and lifelong positive associations between BW and cortical surface area and volume across and within developmental, aging and lifespan longitudinal samples (N = 5794, 4–82 y of age, w/386 monozygotic twins, followed for up to 8.3 y w/12,088 brain MRIs).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the sample size and age range.

claim: The study included 386 monozygotic twins.
source: Here we show remarkably stable and lifelong positive associations between BW and cortical surface area and volume across and within developmental, aging and lifespan longitudinal samples (N = 5794, 4–82 y of age, w/386 monozygotic twins, followed for up to 8.3 y w/12,088 brain MRIs).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the number of monozygotic twins included.

claim: Participants were followed for up to 8.3 years.
source: Here we show remarkably stable and lifelong positive associations between BW and cortical surface area and volume across and within developmental, aging and lifespan longitudinal samples (N = 5794, 4–82 y of age, w/386 monozygotic twins, followed for up to 8.3 y w/12,088 brain MRIs).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the maximum follow-up duration.

claim: The study included 12,088 brain MRIs.
source: Here we show remarkably stable and lifelong positive associations between BW and cortical surface area and volume across and within developmental, aging and lifespan longitudinal samples (N = 5794, 4–82 y of age, w/386 monozygotic twins, followed for up to 8.3 y w/12,088 brain MRIs).
evidence: The abstract explicitly states the total number of brain MRI scans.

claim: Birth weight shows remarkably stable and lifelong positive associations with cortical surface area and volume.
source: Here we show remarkably stable and lifelong positive associations between BW and cortical surface area and volume across and within developmental, aging and lifespan longitudinal samples (N = 5794, 4–82 y of age, w/386 monozygotic twins, followed for up to 8.3 y w/12,088 brain MRIs).
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the data presented in the manuscript.

claim: No consistent effect of birth weight on brain changes was observed.
source: In contrast, no consistent effect of BW on brain changes was observed.
evidence: This is a primary finding stated in the abstract and supported by the longitudinal analyses.

claim: Partly environmental effects of birth weight on brain characteristics were indicated by analysis of twin birth weight discordance.
source: Partly environmental effects were indicated by analysis of twin BW discordance.
evidence: This is a finding from the monozygotic twin analysis presented in the manuscript.

claim: The influence of prenatal growth on cortical topography is stable and reliable through the lifespan.
source: In conclusion, the influence of prenatal growth on cortical topography is stable and reliable through the lifespan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the longitudinal data across multiple cohorts.

claim: Fetal influences appear to affect the brain by association of brain reserve, rather than brain maintenance.
source: This early-life factor appears to influence the brain by association of brain reserve, rather than brain maintenance.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the findings that birth weight affects baseline brain characteristics but not longitudinal changes.

claim: Fetal influences appear omnipresent in the spacetime of the human brain throughout the human lifespan.
source: Thus, fetal influences appear omnipresent in the spacetime of the human brain throughout the human lifespan.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the consistent effects observed across the lifespan.

claim: Optimizing fetal growth may increase brain reserve for life, also in aging.
source: Optimizing fetal growth may increase brain reserve for life, also in aging.
evidence: This is a speculative implication of the findings regarding the persistent effects of birth weight.

claim: A substantial portion of functional variation through the lifespan, including in older age, is of neurodevelopmental origin.
source: It is established that a substantial portion of functional variation through the lifespan, including in older age, is of neurodevelopmental origin (Kovacs et al., 2014; Fjell et al., 2015; Bale, 2015; Muller et al., 2014).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Early-life factors are important for normal individual differences in brain, mental health, and cognition across the lifespan.
source: Evidence converges on early-life factors being important for normal individual differences in brain, mental health, and cognition across the lifespan (Walhovd et al., 2016; Walhovd et al., 2012; Vidal-Pineiro et al., 2021; Dooley et al., 2022; Elliott et al., 2021), as well as risk of psychiatric (Anderson et al., 2021) and neurodegenerative disease in older age (Tuovinen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by multiple citations to prior research.

claim: Early-life factors are associated with risk of psychiatric disease.
source: Evidence converges on early-life factors being important for normal individual differences in brain, mental health, and cognition across the lifespan (Walhovd et al., 2016; Walhovd et al., 2012; Vidal-Pineiro et al., 2021; Dooley et al., 2022; Elliott et al., 2021), as well as risk of psychiatric (Anderson et al., 2021) and neurodegenerative disease in older age (Tuovinen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Anderson et al., 2021.

claim: Early-life factors are associated with risk of neurodegenerative disease in older age.
source: Evidence converges on early-life factors being important for normal individual differences in brain, mental health, and cognition across the lifespan (Walhovd et al., 2016; Walhovd et al., 2012; Vidal-Pineiro et al., 2021; Dooley et al., 2022; Elliott et al., 2021), as well as risk of psychiatric (Anderson et al., 2021) and neurodegenerative disease in older age (Tuovinen et al., 2013).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Tuovinen et al., 2013.

claim: Birth weight reflects fetal and maternal genetic factors.
source: BW reflects fetal and maternal genetic, but also other in utero environmental factors affecting fetal growth (Beaumont et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021; Willis et al., 2022), including brain growth (Walhovd et al., 2012; Raznahan et al., 2012; Casey et al., 2017; Halevy et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Birth weight reflects in utero environmental factors affecting fetal growth.
source: BW reflects fetal and maternal genetic, but also other in utero environmental factors affecting fetal growth (Beaumont et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021; Willis et al., 2022), including brain growth (Walhovd et al., 2012; Raznahan et al., 2012; Casey et al., 2017; Halevy et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Birth weight affects brain growth.
source: BW reflects fetal and maternal genetic, but also other in utero environmental factors affecting fetal growth (Beaumont et al., 2018; Li et al., 2021; Willis et al., 2022), including brain growth (Walhovd et al., 2012; Raznahan et al., 2012; Casey et al., 2017; Halevy et al., 2021).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Birth weight relates positively to mental health.
source: By now, a series of studies have established that BW relates positively to mental health, cognitive function, and brain characteristics, including neuroanatomical volumes and cortical surface area as measured in different age groups (Muller et al., 2014; Walhovd et al., 2016; Walhovd et al., 2012; Raznahan et al., 2012; Wheater et al., 2021; Eriksson et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Birth weight relates positively to cognitive function.
source: By now, a series of studies have established that BW relates positively to mental health, cognitive function, and brain characteristics, including neuroanatomical volumes and cortical surface area as measured in different age groups (Muller et al., 2014; Walhovd et al., 2016; Walhovd et al., 2012; Raznahan et al., 2012; Wheater et al., 2021; Eriksson et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Birth weight relates positively to neuroanatomical volumes.
source: By now, a series of studies have established that BW relates positively to mental health, cognitive function, and brain characteristics, including neuroanatomical volumes and cortical surface area as measured in different age groups (Muller et al., 2014; Walhovd et al., 2016; Walhovd et al., 2012; Raznahan et al., 2012; Wheater et al., 2021; Eriksson et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Birth weight relates positively to cortical surface area.
source: By now, a series of studies have established that BW relates positively to mental health, cognitive function, and brain characteristics, including neuroanatomical volumes and cortical surface area as measured in different age groups (Muller et al., 2014; Walhovd et al., 2016; Walhovd et al., 2012; Raznahan et al., 2012; Wheater et al., 2021; Eriksson et al., 2000).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Cortical surfaces were reconstructed from T1-weighted anatomical MRIs using FreeSurfer v6.0 for LCBC and UKB.
source: Cortical surfaces were reconstructed from T1-weighted anatomical MRIs by use of FreeSurfer v6.0 (LCBC and UKB) and 7.1. (ABCD) (https://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/; Dale et al., 1999; Fischl et al., 2002; Reuter et al., 2012; Jovicich et al., 2013), yielding maps of cortical area, thickness, and volume.
evidence: This describes the image processing methodology used in the study.

claim: Cortical surfaces were reconstructed from T1-weighted anatomical MRIs using FreeSurfer v7.1 for ABCD.
source: Cortical surfaces were reconstructed from T1-weighted anatomical MRIs by use of FreeSurfer v6.0 (LCBC and UKB) and 7.1. (ABCD) (https://surfer.nmr.mgh.harvard.edu/; Dale et al., 1999; Fischl et al., 2002; Reuter et al., 2012; Jovicich et al., 2013), yielding maps of cortical area, thickness, and volume.
evidence: This describes the image processing methodology used in the study.

claim: Vertex-wise analyses were run with spatiotemporal linear mixed effects modeling.
source: Vertex-wise analyses were run with spatiotemporal linear mixed effects modeling (FreeSurfer v6.0.0 ST-MLE package) to assess regional variation in the relationships between BW and cortical structure and its change.
evidence: This describes the statistical analysis method used.

claim: All analyses included baseline age, sex, scanner site, and time as covariates.
source: All analyses were run with baseline age, sex, scanner site, and time (scan interval) as covariates.
evidence: This describes the covariates controlled for in the analyses.

claim: For ABCD, ethnicity was included as a covariate.
source: For ABCD specifically, ethnicity was also included as a covariate.
evidence: This describes an additional covariate used in the ABCD sample analyses.

claim: Widespread positive associations were observed between birth weight and cortical area across all cohorts.
source: Across all cohorts, widespread positive associations were observed between BW and cortical area.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the vertex-wise analyses presented in Figure 1.

claim: Birth weight associations with cortical area were highly consistent across lifespan, developmental, and aging cohorts.
source: These were highly consistent across lifespan (LCBC), developmental (ABCD), and aging (UKB) cohorts, and there were bilateral overlapping effects across most of the cortical mantle.
evidence: This describes the consistency of findings across different cohorts.

claim: Birth weight had lesser effects on cortical thickness compared to cortical area.
source: As expected, BW had, in general, lesser effects on cortical thickness and no significant effects on thickness were observed in the UKB.
evidence: This is a finding from the vertex-wise analyses comparing effects on different cortical measures.

claim: No significant effects of birth weight on cortical thickness were observed in the UKB cohort.
source: As expected, BW had, in general, lesser effects on cortical thickness and no significant effects on thickness were observed in the UKB.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the UKB cohort analysis.

claim: Birth weight was significantly positively associated with cortical volume across much of the cortical mantle.
source: BW was significantly positively associated with cortical volume across much of the cortical mantle.
evidence: This is a primary finding from the vertex-wise analyses.

claim: Controlling for education level had little effect on the results.
source: Additionally controlling for education level had little effect on results (see Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analyses shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Controlling for gestational age in subsamples had relatively little effect on results.
source: Controlling for gestational age in these subsamples had relatively little effect on results (see Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analyses shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: When restricting samples to participants with birth weight between 2.5 and 5.0 kg, results were very similar.
source: When restricting all samples to participants with BW between 2.5 and 5.0 kg, results were also very similar (see Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is a finding from sensitivity analyses shown in a supplementary figure.

claim: Consistent significant positive effects of birth weight on cortical area when controlling for intracranial volume were observed across all three cohorts in lateral temporal and frontal areas.
source: However, consistent significant positive effects of BW on cortical area also when controlling for ICV were observed across all three cohorts in lateral temporal and frontal areas.
evidence: This is a finding from analyses controlling for intracranial volume.

claim: Significant birth weight × time interactions on cortical characteristics were observed in restricted and non-overlapping regions across samples.
source: Significant BW × time interactions on cortical characteristics were observed in restricted and non-overlapping regions across samples (see Figure 2 [depicting right hemisphere results]; for visualization of effects in both hemispheres, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal interaction analyses.

claim: The effect of birth weight differences was apparently reduced over time for cortical area in LCBC and ABCD.
source: Per direction of effect, the effect of BW differences was apparently reduced over time for area in LCBC and ABCD, whereas no interaction effects on area were significant in UKB.
evidence: This describes the direction of interaction effects observed in specific cohorts.

claim: No interaction effects of birth weight on cortical area were significant in UKB.
source: Per direction of effect, the effect of BW differences was apparently reduced over time for area in LCBC and ABCD, whereas no interaction effects on area were significant in UKB.
evidence: This is a specific finding from the UKB cohort longitudinal analysis.

claim: All spatial comparisons of birth weight effects on cortical structure across datasets were statistically significant.
source: The results showed that all the spatial comparisons were statistically significant (p<0.05, FDR-corrected).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial correlation analyses comparing cortical maps across cohorts.

claim: The topography of birth weight effects on cortical structure was comparable across datasets.
source: That is, the topography of the effects of BW on cortical structure was comparable across datasets – the pairwise spatial correlation of a given cortical correlate of BW (e.g., BW effects on cortical area) was similar when estimated from two different datasets.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the spatial correlation results.

claim: Spatial correlations of birth weight effects on cortical volume were highest (r = 0.64–0.79).
source: The spatial correlations were the highest for the volume measures (r = 0.64–0.79), and overall also high (r = 0.51–0.71) for area measures, whereas for cortical thickness, they were more moderate (r = 0.24–0.45).
evidence: This reports specific correlation values from the spatial correlation analyses.

claim: Spatial correlations of birth weight effects on cortical area were high (r = 0.51–0.71).
source: The spatial correlations were the highest for the volume measures (r = 0.64–0.79), and overall also high (r = 0.51–0.71) for area measures, whereas for cortical thickness, they were more moderate (r = 0.24–0.45).
evidence: This reports specific correlation values from the spatial correlation analyses.

claim: Spatial correlations of birth weight effects on cortical thickness were moderate (r = 0.24–0.45).
source: The spatial correlations were the highest for the volume measures (r = 0.64–0.79), and overall also high (r = 0.51–0.71) for area measures, whereas for cortical thickness, they were more moderate (r = 0.24–0.45).
evidence: This reports specific correlation values from the spatial correlation analyses.

claim: The spatial correlation of maps capturing birth weight-associated cortical change was either unrelated or showed negative associations between cohorts.
source: In contrast, the spatial correlation of the maps capturing BW-associated cortical change (i.e., BW × time contrast) was either unrelated (n = 7) or showed negative associations between cohorts (n = 2).
evidence: This is a finding from the spatial correlation analyses of longitudinal change effects.

claim: Birth weight discordance was associated with cortical area, where the heavier twins had greater area in some frontal, temporal, and occipitotemporal regions.
source: BW discordance was associated with cortical area, where the heavier twins had greater area in some frontal, temporal, and occipitotemporal regions, with effects in the right hemisphere only surviving corrections for multiple comparisons.
evidence: This is a finding from the monozygotic twin discordance analysis.

claim: Birth weight discordance effects on cortical area in the right hemisphere survived corrections for multiple comparisons.
source: BW discordance was associated with cortical area, where the heavier twins had greater area in some frontal, temporal, and occipitotemporal regions, with effects in the right hemisphere only surviving corrections for multiple comparisons.
evidence: This specifies which effects survived statistical correction in the twin analysis.

claim: There was no association of birth weight discordance and cortical area changes over time.
source: There was no association of BW discordance and cortical area changes over time.
evidence: This is a finding from the longitudinal twin discordance analysis.

claim: Birth weight discordance had a significant negative effect on cortical thickness in restricted right frontotemporal regions.
source: BW discordance also had a significant negative effect on cortical thickness in restricted right frontotemporal regions, where being the lighter twin yielded greater thickness.
evidence: This is a finding from the monozygotic twin discordance analysis.

claim: Being the lighter twin yielded greater cortical thickness in restricted right frontotemporal regions.
source: BW discordance also had a significant negative effect on cortical thickness in restricted right frontotemporal regions, where being the lighter twin yielded greater thickness.
evidence: This describes the direction of the effect in the twin discordance analysis.

claim: There were no significant effects of birth weight discordance on cortical volume or volume change over time.
source: There were no significant effects of BW discordance on cortical volume or volume change over time.
evidence: This is a finding from the twin discordance analysis.

claim: The effect of 1 SD difference in birth weight on cortical volume was 6708 mm³ in LCBC.
source: The effect of 1 SD lower BW on cortical volume was 6708 mm3, 8466 mm3, and 5980 mm3 in LCBC, UKB, and ABCD, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated effect size from the data.

claim: The effect of 1 SD difference in birth weight on cortical volume was 8466 mm³ in UKB.
source: The effect of 1 SD lower BW on cortical volume was 6708 mm3, 8466 mm3, and 5980 mm3 in LCBC, UKB, and ABCD, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated effect size from the data.

claim: The effect of 1 SD difference in birth weight on cortical volume was 5980 mm³ in ABCD.
source: The effect of 1 SD lower BW on cortical volume was 6708 mm3, 8466 mm3, and 5980 mm3 in LCBC, UKB, and ABCD, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated effect size from the data.

claim: 1 SD lower birth weight equals 1.2% lesser cortex in LCBC.
source: This was equal to 1.2, 1.6, and 1.1% lesser cortex with 600–700 g lower BW for each sample, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated percentage from the effect size data.

claim: 1 SD lower birth weight equals 1.6% lesser cortex in UKB.
source: This was equal to 1.2, 1.6, and 1.1% lesser cortex with 600–700 g lower BW for each sample, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated percentage from the effect size data.

claim: 1 SD lower birth weight equals 1.1% lesser cortex in ABCD.
source: This was equal to 1.2, 1.6, and 1.1% lesser cortex with 600–700 g lower BW for each sample, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated percentage from the effect size data.

claim: The estimated yearly cortical volume reduction from 50 to 60 years is 895 mm³ in LCBC.
source: The estimated yearly cortical volume reduction from 50 to 60 y is 895 mm3 in the LCBC and 1402 mm3 in the UKB samples, respectively.
evidence: This is an estimated rate of change from the longitudinal data.

claim: The estimated yearly cortical volume reduction from 50 to 60 years is 1402 mm³ in UKB.
source: The estimated yearly cortical volume reduction from 50 to 60 y is 895 mm3 in the LCBC and 1402 mm3 in the UKB samples, respectively.
evidence: This is an estimated rate of change from the longitudinal data.

claim: The effect of 600 g difference in birth weight could be quantitatively equal to that of 7.5 years of estimated age differences in LCBC.
source: Hence, the effect of 600 g difference in BW could, if only cross-sectional data were available, be quantitatively equal to that of 7.5 and 6 y of estimated age differences in LCBC and UKB, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated comparison of effect sizes.

claim: The effect of 600 g difference in birth weight could be quantitatively equal to that of 6 years of estimated age differences in UKB.
source: Hence, the effect of 600 g difference in BW could, if only cross-sectional data were available, be quantitatively equal to that of 7.5 and 6 y of estimated age differences in LCBC and UKB, respectively.
evidence: This is a calculated comparison of effect sizes.

claim: Birth weight shows robust, persistent, and chiefly stable associations with brain characteristics through life.
source: The present results indicate that BW, the earliest widely and easily obtainable congenital metric, shows robust, persistent, and chiefly stable associations with brain characteristics through life.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion from the study findings.

claim: Birth weight was associated with cortical area and volume in an age and time-invariant fashion.
source: Especially, BW was associated with cortical area and volume in an age and time-invariant fashion.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding regarding the stability of effects.

claim: Birth weight appears to have the most replicable and consistent relations to cortical morphology besides BMI.
source: BW stands out as the single chronological earliest phenotype, and besides BMI, BW appears to have the most replicable and consistent relations to cortical morphology, as shown here both across and within samples.
evidence: This is a comparative conclusion based on the replicability analyses and comparison to prior literature.

claim: Birth weight differences have been reported for neurodevelopmental disorders such as ADHD.
source: As noted, BW differences have been reported for neurodevelopmental disorders such as attention deficit hyperactovity disorder (ADHD) (Momany et al., 2018), and also other neurodevelopmental disorders, such as schizophrenia or more general psychopathology, with the cortical effects detected not invariably being very large in absolute terms (Patel et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Birth weight differences have been reported for schizophrenia.
source: As noted, BW differences have been reported for neurodevelopmental disorders such as attention deficit hyperactovity disorder (ADHD) (Momany et al., 2018), and also other neurodevelopmental disorders, such as schizophrenia or more general psychopathology, with the cortical effects detected not invariably being very large in absolute terms (Patel et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Patel et al., 2022.

claim: The data indicate that any effect of birth weight on cortical change may be of relatively more temporary nature.
source: Thus, the data seem to indicate that any effect of BW on cortical change may be of relatively more temporary nature.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the longitudinal findings.

claim: The 'offset effect' of birth weight on cortical area and volume appears persistent and consistent across the lifespan.
source: The 'offset effect' of BW, on the other hand, appears persistent and consistent, especially in terms of stable and widespread effects on cortical area and volume across the lifespan.
evidence: This is a summary interpretation of the main findings.

claim: Recent findings indicate that effects of exposure to environmental adversity on epigenetic programming in aging may be localized to the in utero period.
source: Interestingly, however, recent findings indicate that the effects of exposure to environmental adversity on epigenetic programming in aging may be localized to the in utero period (Schmitz and Duque, 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Schmitz and Duque, 2022.

claim: Neurogenesis takes place almost only in fetal development.
source: For instance, neurogenesis takes place almost only in fetal development (Rakic, 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rakic, 1988.

claim: Adult human neurogenesis must be severely restricted in location and amount.
source: Even if controversies remain, evidence suggests that any adult human neurogenesis must be severely restricted in location and amount (Bhardwaj et al., 2006; Paredes et al., 2016).
evidence: This statement is supported by citations to prior research.

claim: Human beings are born with almost all cortical neurons they will have through life.
source: Thus, human beings appear to be born with almost all cortical neurons they will have through life, and neuronal migration and differentiation are also defined early, by the place and time the neuron is born during fetal life (Rakic, 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation and represents established neuroscience knowledge.

claim: Neuronal migration and differentiation are defined early by the place and time the neuron is born during fetal life.
source: Thus, human beings appear to be born with almost all cortical neurons they will have through life, and neuronal migration and differentiation are also defined early, by the place and time the neuron is born during fetal life (Rakic, 1988).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rakic, 1988.

claim: Animal studies of chronic placental insufficiency have shown effects on brain development that persist with age.
source: Animal studies of chronic placental insufficiency have shown effects on brain development that persist with age (Rehn et al., 2004).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Rehn et al., 2004.

claim: About 200 million children in developing countries are not meeting their growth potential.
source: About 200 million children in developing countries are not meeting their growth potential, and improving the prenatal environment is likely important to help children reach their full potential (McGovern, 2019) – and ultimately also to help them stay above a functional threshold into older age.
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to McGovern, 2019.

claim: In utero opioid exposure is associated with higher risk of fetal growth restriction.
source: The opioid epidemic is increasingly affecting pregnant women, and in utero opioid exposure is associated with higher risk of fetal growth restriction (Azuine et al., 2019).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Azuine et al., 2019.

claim: Local traffic congestion-pollution exposure during pregnancy was associated with reductions in term birth weight in a large US sample.
source: Recently, local traffic congestion-pollution exposure during pregnancy, independently of a series of maternal sociodemographic characteristics, was associated with reductions in term BW in a large US sample (Willis et al., 2022).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Willis et al., 2022.

claim: Programs and policies to limit environmental factors reducing fetal growth may enhance brain reserve and prevent more people from falling below a functional threshold in advanced age.
source: Programs and policies to limit such environmental factors reducing fetal growth may thus enhance brain reserve and ultimately prevent more people from falling below a functional threshold even in advanced age.
evidence: This is a speculative policy implication based on the study findings.

claim: There was a very high correlation between registry and self-reported birth weight in LCBC.
source: While there was a very high correlation between registry and self-reported BW in LCBC, this is a possible source of noise.
evidence: This is a validation finding regarding the birth weight measurement.

claim: A high reliability of self-reported birth weight over time has been found in broader Norwegian Twin Registry samples.
source: A high reliability of self-reported BW over time has also been found in broader NTR samples (Nilsen et al., 2017).
evidence: This statement is supported by a citation to Nilsen et al., 2017.

claim: In total, longitudinal data for 5718 persons with 12,088 MRI scans from the LCBC, ABCD, and UKB studies were included in the analyses.
source: In total, longitudinal data for 5718 persons with 12,088 MRI scans from the LCBC, ABCD, and UKB studies were included in the analyses.
evidence: This describes the total sample size for the main analyses.

claim: Only persons with longitudinal MRI scans were included in the main analyses to limit the possibility that estimates of change were biased by immediate sample selection effects.
source: Only persons with longitudinal MRI scans were included in the main analyses to limit the possibility that estimates of change were biased by immediate sample selection effects (i.e., those that remain for follow-up are known to have other characteristics than those who have only one time point assessment in longitudinal studies, and this can bias effects).
evidence: This explains the rationale for the inclusion criteria.

claim: The LCBC sample included 635 participants with 1922 scans.
evidence: This information is provided in Table 1.

claim: The ABCD sample included 3324 participants with 6648 scans.
evidence: This information is provided in Table 1.

claim: The UKB sample included 1759 participants with 3518 scans.
evidence: This information is provided in Table 1.

claim: The mean baseline age in LCBC was 19.1 years (SD = 20.7, range = 4.1–81.9).
evidence: This information is provided in Table 1.

claim: The mean baseline age in ABCD was 10.0 years (SD = 0.6, range = 8.9–11.1).
evidence: This information is provided in Table 1.

claim: The mean baseline age in UKB was 62.0 years (SD = 7.1, range = 47–80.3).
evidence: This information is provided in Table 1.

claim: The mean birth weight in LCBC was 3.5 kg (SD = 0.6, range = 0.9–6.0).
evidence: This information is provided in Table 1.

claim: The mean birth weight in ABCD was 3.2 kg (SD = 0.7, range = 1.0–6.7).
evidence: This information is provided in Table 1.

claim: The mean birth weight in UKB was 3.4 kg (SD = 0.6, range = 0.9–6.4).
evidence: This information is provided in Table 1.

claim: Widespread positive associations between birth weight and cortical area are shown in Figure 1 for the right hemisphere.
source: Associations of BW and cortical characteristics are shown in Figure 1 (for the right hemisphere) and in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 (for both hemispheres).
evidence: This references the figure showing the main results.

claim: Birth weight effects on cortical change are shown in Figure 2 for the right hemisphere.
source: To test the effect of BW on cortical change, we reran the analyses with BW × time and age × time interactions. Note that BW × time (i.e., within-subject follow-up time) represents the contrasts of interest while age – and age interactions – is used to account for the differences in age across individuals. Significant BW × time interactions on cortical characteristics were observed in restricted and non-overlapping regions across samples (see Figure 2 [depicting right hemisphere results]; for visualization of effects in both hemispheres, see Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
evidence: This references the figure showing the longitudinal interaction results.

claim: Spatial correlation of birth weight effects on brain structure across datasets is shown in Figure 3.
source: See spatial correlations for the right hemisphere cortical volume in Figure 3 and the full model summary in Supplementary file 1.
evidence: This references the figure showing the spatial correlation results.

claim: Birth weight discordance effects on cortical area in monozygotic twins are shown in Figure 4.
source: BW discordance was associated with cortical area, where the heavier twins had greater area in some frontal, temporal, and occipitotemporal regions, with effects in the right hemisphere only surviving corrections for multiple comparisons. We note that these regions mostly overlap with regions where positive effects of BW were also seen in the bigger sample. Strikingly, the effect of BW discordance, as shown in Figure 4, appeared similar in size to the effect of BW itself in the MZ twin sample.
evidence: This references the figure showing the twin discordance results for cortical area.

claim: Birth weight discordance effects on cortical thickness in monozygotic twins are shown in Figure 5.
source: BW discordance also had a significant negative effect on cortical thickness in restricted right frontotemporal regions, where being the lighter twin yielded greater thickness. These significant effects did not appear to overlap with regions where significant negative associations with BW were seen in the bigger sample. BW had little effect on cortical thickness in the significant region, and the effect of BW discordance in the identified regions, as shown in Figure 5, appeared greater than the effect of BW itself here in the MZ twin sample.
evidence: This references the figure showing the twin discordance results for cortical thickness.
